stem: A bond has a face value of Rs 1,000, a coupon rate of 8% per annum paid annually, and matures in exactly 1 year. The required rate of return is 10% per annum. What is the intrinsic value (fair price) of the bond today?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Cash flow at end of year 1 = coupon + face value = 80 + 1000 = 1080. PV = 1080 / 1.10 = 981.82.
Equates bond value with face value (Rs 1,000), ignoring that the required return (10%) differs from the coupon rate (8%), so the bond must trade at a discount.
Reports the total cash flow (Rs 1,080) without discounting it, i.e. treats future value as present value.
Discounts only the face value (1000/1.10 = 909) without adding the discounted coupon (80/1.10 = 72.73), giving 909 + 0 = 909 or subtracts discount differently, landing on Rs 960.

explanation: Bond value = PV of all future cash flows discounted at the required rate. For a 1-year bond: value = (coupon + face) / (1 + r) = (80 + 1000) / 1.10 = 1080 / 1.10 = Rs 981.82.

explanation_sections.punchline: A bond trading at a discount means the required return exceeds the coupon rate; the fair price is the PV of coupon plus face value.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify: single-period bond. Total cash flow at maturity = coupon + face = 1000*0.08 + 1000 = 1080. Discount at required return: PV = 1080/1.10 = 981.82.
explanation_sections.lesson: When required return > coupon rate, bond value < face value (discount bond). Always discount total cash flows, not just coupons.
explanation_sections.timing: 40 seconds. One multiplication and one division. Trap: forgetting to discount the face value along with the coupon.
